column1: # What Felix refuses on itself.
# Deliberately short. Felix governs projects in languages it must not require
# and should be equally slow to invent rules for them; these are two its own
# constitution already states and nothing enforced.
# tool
# A fourth column, `checkout`, says a row protects the governed checkout and
# nothing else: a match is passed over when everything the matched command acts
# on is a throwaway fixture under /tmp or $TMPDIR, and stands otherwise,
# including whenever that cannot be told (lib/where.sh). The rows below
# carrying it guard three things: the binding (four rows, since #311 split one
# row by how a command writes), the remote-tracking refs and the remote. On
# 2026-09-23 those three were most of the refusals the hooks had logged: a
# fixture repository bound with `printf ... > .felix`, a fresh `git init`
# given a remote, a scratch clone's remote-tracking refs moved. Each protects
# this checkout's binding, remote or refs, and no fixture's.
Bash
column3: force push drops commits, and Felix's history is the audit trail

column1: # The binding, which is the one surface a refusal has to protect from the
# inside. `.felix` names which project governs a checkout and
# `$HOME/.felix-home` names which home that project is resolved against;
# break either and every hook in every session resolves nothing. The Stop
# hook now refuses a binding that is present and does not resolve, but that
# fires after the damage, and the pointer is worse than the marker because
# it sits outside every repository — no diff, no classification, nothing at
# a merge boundary to see. This is the only enforcing row it can have.
# Reading either is still allowed. What is refused is writing one by hand,
# because `felix new` and `felix install` write them and say what they did.
Write

column1: # The path may be quoted, and the command may go on after it with `;`, `&&`,
# `|` or a closing paren. The first spelling required a space or the end of
# the line after the name, so a quoted marker and a marker followed by `;`
# both walked past it. A row that ordinary redirect spellings step around is
# a row that refuses only the person who wrote it.
# It was one row until 2026-09-23, and that row refused reads. Its verbs had
# no word start, so the `ln ` in `grep -rln '\.felix'` was a link; its `>`
# matched `2>/dev/null` and ran on to a later READ of the pointer, in the
# `tr -d '[:space:]' 2>/dev/null < "$HOME/.felix-home"` the engine itself
# resolves the home with; and `cp .felix /tmp/backup` copies the marker
# somewhere else. Each was reproduced with argv-logging shims and a hash of
# the marker and the pointer, and each is in the logged refusals. So a row
# for each way a command writes a file:
#   - a redirect writes its own target word, so the marker must be that word,
#     quoted or not, and not something later in the command. A target quoted
#     round a blank is still one word, and the second reading in lib/deny.sh
#     drops its quotes, so the second redirect row lets the target run across
#     blanks: only where the `>` is an operator (at the start of a line, or
#     after a blank, a digit, `;`, `&`, `|` or `(`), only over pieces that
#     start with no `-` and hold no quote, where every piece after the first
#     starts with no `/`, `~`, `$` or `.`, each of which begins a path of its
#     own, and only to a marker that ends a path;
#   - tee, mv, rm, truncate and sed -i write the files they name, so the
#     marker among their operands is a write, unless a `<` before it makes
#     it what they read; dd writes the file its of= names;
#   - cp, scp, ln and install write their last operand, so the marker is a
#     write there, and a read before it unless that last operand is a
#     directory, where the copy lands as a marker of its own: `.`, `..`, or a
#     path ending in `/`. A directory named without the slash cannot be told
#     from a file by reading the command, and is let through.
# A verb is a word, never the tail of one: it starts a line, or the character
# before it is not a letter, digit, `_`, `.` or `-`, so `-rln` and `-ln` are
# flags again. A row reads the payload's JSON string, where a line break or a
# tab is a backslash and an `n`, `r` or `t`, so those are named on their own,
# at the start of a verb and at the end of a marker, and only unescaped: a
# `\n` typed inside quoted text arrives as two backslashes and an `n`, and is
# no line break. The first drafts of these rows let a write on a later line,
# or on a tab-indented one, go through, which the old row had refused. A
# comment may follow the last operand. scp is named because the old row
# caught it only as the tail `cp `.
Bash
column3: rewriting the binding by hand is how the floor gets switched off in one line; use felix new or felix install --home

column1: # The next row is not about damage to the tree. It is about a command shape
# that hangs the session that ran it, which this project learned on 2026-09-12
# after 22 of them in one session left spinning shells and 34 stray helper
# processes behind, some alive for more than a day.
# Measured in both shells, from a probe rather than from a manual:
# `read -t 5 -r _ < <(tail -f /dev/null)` returns after 5.0s under bash and
# NEVER returns under zsh — still blocked when a twelve-second cap killed it —
# and both leave the helper process running. Sessions here run zsh. A wait
# written this way does not time out, never advances its own counter, and is
# moved to the background by the tool's own timeout, where it spins until
# something kills it.
# There is no good use of it. Work that must be waited on runs as a background
# job, whose completion notifies the session, or under a monitor.
Bash
column3: a timed read from a process substitution never returns under zsh and leaks its helper; run the work as a background job and wait for its completion instead

column1: # The exception table (amendments §3) is read from refs/remotes/origin/main, so
# that a grant takes effect only by being merged where a person decides. Two
# named commands would let a session move that ref itself — writing a
# remote-tracking ref, fetching a refspec into one, rewriting the remote,
# pushing main — and each is refused here, global options tolerated. A regex
# over command text refuses the spellings it names and no other; branch
# protection on the remote is the rule that cannot be evaded from here at
# all, and until it exists these are the floor, not the wall.
# Only a ref written is refused. Until 2026-09-23 one row refused
# refs/remotes/ anywhere after update-ref or symbolic-ref, and so refused
# commands that only read one: `git update-ref refs/heads/backup
# refs/remotes/origin/main` writes refs/heads/backup, and `git symbolic-ref
# --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD` prints. Both were written blind as
# allowed that day. Each row below is matched against lib/deny.sh's reading
# of the command, where quotes round a word are gone and each separator is a
# token of its own:
#   - update-ref writes its first operand, and the others are values it
#     reads. Passed on the way to it: options, -m and its reason, and
#     redirects, a bare `>` with the word it writes to.
#   - symbolic-ref with one operand prints it. With two it points the first
#     at the second, and a ref pointed at a remote-tracking ref moves it on
#     the next commit, so either operand refuses. -d or --delete deletes its
#     one operand. The final operand has to end at a blank, so the 2 of
#     2>/dev/null is not taken for one.
#   - fetch and push name refs/remotes/ only in a refspec that writes one,
#     so any mention there is refused, as before. A plain fetch names none.
# None of them sees a ref named only on update-ref --stdin's input: a
# here-document body or a printed line is data to the reading.
Bash
column3: a remote-tracking ref is what the remote said, and the exception table is read from it; only a plain fetch may move it

column1: # A pattern kill reaches every process on the machine whose name or command
# line matches, and this machine runs several sessions' suites at once. Twice an
# agent killed by pattern although its prompt forbade it, on 2026-09-25
# (`pkill -f 'engine/harness/tests/run'`) and on 2026-10-18 (`pkill -f 'sleep
# 3'`), and each time the pattern reached other sessions' runs. A prompt did not
# hold, so this row does, by the founder's decision of 2026-10-19. The contract,
# its two amendments and the limits below are in
# audits/2026-10-19-pattern-kill-deny/contract.md.
# A command's position is the start, after a separator, after a case pattern's
# `)` or after find's -exec, and then after any of then, do, else, time, if,
# while, until and !. A wrapper may come first (VAR=val, a redirect, sudo, env,
# nice, timeout, xargs, nohup, time, exec, command, watch and a few more), and
# any path may lead the command word. At such a position, this row refuses:
#   - killall;
#   - pkill, unless a word binds it to a pid. -F binds it, and so does -P with
#     a parent list that does not hold 1, since 1 is every orphan's parent. A
#     -P whose pid comes from a pgrep does not;
#   - pids from a pgrep that no pid binds, handed to kill: kill $(pgrep ...),
#     pgrep ... | xargs kill, pgrep ... | while read p; do kill $p, and
#     p=$(pgrep ...) or for p in $(pgrep ...) followed by kill $p. Inside a
#     -c script, kill $(pgrep ...) and the pipe forms are refused too; the
#     variable and loop forms are not.
# A quoted pattern is one word. The reading prints every separator as a token
# with blanks round it, so a `|` glued inside a word came from quotes. Two
# things are not pattern kills here: kill -0 and kill -s 0 send no signal, and a
# pgrep piped to wc prints a count, not pids.
# The reading appends each substitution's body after the text, so a pgrep in
# a substitution is matched as the last body appended. That causes two limits,
# which this row keeps rather than buy a regex that counts:
#   - a kill whose pgrep body is not the last one is missed, as in
#     `kill $(pgrep -f x) || echo "none at $(date)"`;
#   - a command that kills by pid and ends with a check like "$(pgrep -fl x)"
#     is refused. Run the check as its own command.
# As with every row, this one does not see a command built at run time, a
# command word with a backslash in it, or text piped into a shell. It refuses,
# although nothing is harmed, `; pkill` inside a quoted sed, cp, rm or touch
# operand, which the reading keeps, and remote forms such as ssh host 'pkill
# Measured on 2026-10-19 over the 4705 distinct commands naming kill in this
# machine's transcripts:
#   - It refuses 173. Of those, 159 are a pkill -f, a kill fed by pgrep -f, or
#     a pgrep -f piped to xargs kill; 12 kill pgrep's pids through a variable
#     or a loop; and 2 are pid-tree kills ending in a check, the second limit
#     above.
#   - Drafts that refused more taught the exceptions: 23 pkill -P and 1 pgrep -P
#     tree kills, 3 kill -0 waits, and a tree kill counted with pgrep | wc.
#   - CPU: about 1 ms per Bash call however short the command, most of it bash
#     compiling the pattern; the longest row before it costs 0.1 ms. On a
#     30,000-character reading of plain words it costs about 14 ms. The eight
#     longest commands in the corpus read under 430 characters.
Bash
column3: a pattern kill reaches other sessions' runs on this machine; kill only the pid you started ($! or a pidfile): STOP then KILL the root, then its tree by pid
